title: Zechariah in the temple (Luke 1:5–17)
hookLine: an old priest's prayer is answered at last in the holy place

lines: AN OLD PRIEST AND HIS WIFE.
NO CHILD, AND NOW TOO OLD.
cards: Luke's story doesn't open in a palace, or even in Nazareth. It opens with an elderly couple who have done everything right.
In the King James Bible: "There was in the days of Herod, the king of Judaea, a certain priest named Zacharias." That's the Greek form of Zechariah. His wife Elisabeth is from a priestly family too.

Both righteous, Luke says, walking in all the commandments blameless. Then the line that hurts: "they had no child, because that Elisabeth was barren, and they both were now well stricken in years." Good people.
Faithful people. And the one thing they prayed for never came.

teach.h: THE LOT FALLS: INCENSE IN THE HOLY PLACE.
teach.b: Zechariah's priestly division is on duty in Jerusalem, and by lot, the custom of the priest's office, he is chosen to go into the temple of the Lord and burn incense.
Jewish tradition later recorded that a priest might get that honor only once in his life. So an old man stands alone at the altar of incense, smoke rising, while outside the whole crowd prays.
Suddenly an angel is standing at the right side of the altar. Zechariah is terrified.

teach.h: FEAR NOT: THY PRAYER IS HEARD.
teach.b: The angel's first words: "Fear not, Zacharias: for thy prayer is heard; and thy wife Elisabeth shall bear thee a son, and thou shalt call his name John." Which prayer?
Probably the one for a child, prayed for decades, maybe given up on years ago. Some readers also hear the prayer for Israel's rescue he was offering that very hour.
Some hear the names too: Zechariah is usually taken to mean the LORD has remembered, and John, God is gracious.
Then the child's job: to go before the Lord "in the spirit and power of Elias, to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children."
That echoes the closing lines of Malachi, heard seven days ago, the last book of the prophets in Christian Bibles. In Luke's telling, that waiting is over.
Christians hear the whole Gospel starting here: not with fanfare, but with a faithful old man whose prayer was heard.

how: Some churches read the story of Zechariah in the weeks before Christmas, and Catholic and Orthodox Christians honor Zechariah and Elizabeth as saints.

games.q: you're Zechariah, old, alone in the holy place, burning incense. an angel appears beside the altar. what are his first words to you?
o: you have been chosen to lead Israel.
fear not: thy prayer is heard.
games.why: "fear not, Zacharias: for thy prayer is heard." a prayer prayed for decades, maybe given up on, answered in the holy place.

practice: Bring to mind something you hoped or prayed for long ago and quietly stopped asking about: a healing, a reconciliation, a child, a door that never opened.
Take it out and look at it again, the way Zechariah might have with the incense rising, and notice whether there's hope in you, or tiredness, or both.
If you pray, offer that old prayer to God again, as honestly as you can; if not, hold the hope gently for these minutes.

carryVoice: Your line: your prayer is heard. An old man, an old prayer, and the Gospel begins. See you tomorrow.
